easy.prompt: What does O(n log n) describe?

choices.label: A
choices.body: An upper bound on a function's growth rate, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A lower bound on a function's growth rate.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The exact number of operations an algorithm performs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The average number of operations across random inputs.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Big-O is a worst-case upper bound up to constant factors; it tells you the function grows no faster than n log n for large n.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's Big-Ω. Big-O is an upper bound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Big-O hides constants and lower-order terms; it isn't an exact count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's average-case analysis; Big-O on its own is worst-case asymptotic.

easy.prompt: Which sort runs in O(n log n) worst case and uses O(1) extra space (excluding recursion stack)?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Heapsort builds a heap in place and repeatedly extracts the max, giving deterministic O(n log n) with O(1) extra space.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) worst case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mergesort is O(n log n) but needs O(n) auxiliary space for the merge buffer.

easy.prompt: Which property is true of a stable sort?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Equal-keyed elements keep their original relative order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It always runs in linear time.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Stability means two records with the same key appear in the output in the same order they appeared in the input.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Many stable sorts (e.g., merge sort) use comparisons.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stability says nothing about memory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stability is unrelated to running time.

easy.prompt: What is the worst-case time to find an element in a balanced binary search tree of n nodes?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A balanced BST has height Θ(log n), and search descends one level at a time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a typical sort cost, not search.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Constant-time lookup is a hash-table property, not a BST.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the worst case for an unbalanced (degenerate) BST.

easy.prompt: Which operation is O(1) amortized on a dynamic array (e.g., Python list, C++ vector)?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Doubling the backing array makes the amortized cost per append constant, even though some appends trigger an O(n) resize.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Mid-deletion also shifts elements — Θ(n).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That requires selection (Θ(n)) or a sorted structure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Front insertion shifts every element — Θ(n).

easy.prompt: BFS from a source in an unweighted graph computes which property of every reachable vertex?

choices.label: B
choices.body: The minimum number of edges from the source.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A minimum spanning tree of the graph.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The minimum total edge weight from the source.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of edge-count distance, so it yields shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Topological order comes from DFS on a DAG.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MSTs are computed with Kruskal or Prim.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weighted shortest paths need Dijkstra or Bellman–Ford.

easy.prompt: Which algorithm computes single-source shortest paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Dijkstra greedily settles the nearest unvisited vertex; correctness relies on non-negative weights.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Topological sort orders a DAG; it isn't a shortest-path algorithm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree, not shortest paths.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Floyd–Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths, not single-source.

easy.prompt: The recurrence T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n) solves to which closed form?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: By the Master Theorem, a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n falls in case 2, so T(n) = Θ(n log n) — exactly the mergesort recurrence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Linear time would require the merge step to be sublinear.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Logarithmic time would imply constant work per level, but each level here does Θ(n) work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the quicksort worst case; this recurrence is balanced.

easy.prompt: What is the expected time to look up a key in a hash table with a good hash function and load factor under 1?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: With uniform hashing and bounded load factor, the expected probe count is constant.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a sort cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Linear is the worst case if every key collides, not the expectation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's tree-based search, not hashing.

easy.prompt: When does a greedy algorithm provably yield an optimal solution?

choices.label: C
choices.body: When the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Whenever the answer is a number.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Greedy correctness requires that a locally optimal choice extends to a global optimum (greedy choice) and that subproblems can be solved independently (optimal substructure).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sorted input helps efficiency but doesn't justify greedy correctness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Greedy applies far beyond graphs (e.g., Huffman coding, scheduling).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Numerical output is unrelated to whether greedy is correct.

easy.prompt: What is the central idea of dynamic programming?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pick the locally best option at each step.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Solve and memoize overlapping subproblems so each is computed only once.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Repeatedly halve the input until it fits in cache.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Restart from scratch whenever the answer changes.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: DP exploits overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by caching results in a table.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's greedy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's divide-and-conquer (without memoization).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DP avoids recomputation — the opposite of restarting.

easy.prompt: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-hard?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It has no known algorithm at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It can be solved in polynomial time.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: NP-hardness is defined by polynomial-time reductions from every NP problem; the hard problem need not itself be in NP.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Many NP-hard problems have algorithms — just none known to run in polynomial time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: If an NP-hard problem were in P, then P = NP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Hardness is about time reductions, not space.

easy.prompt: Which traversal naturally produces a topological order on a DAG?

choices.label: D
choices.body: DFS, emitting each vertex when its recursion returns (post-order, reversed).

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: DFS post-order finishes a vertex only after all its descendants, so reversing the finishing order yields a topological sort.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: BFS gives shortest-edge-count layers, not a topological order.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Union-find tracks connectivity; it doesn't order vertices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dijkstra computes shortest paths; it doesn't order DAG vertices.

easy.prompt: What invariant does binary search maintain on each iteration?

choices.label: A
choices.body: If the target exists in the array, it lies within the current [lo, hi] window.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The window length doubles each step.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every element in the window is equal to the target.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The array is partitioned around a pivot.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Binary search shrinks the candidate window by half each step while preserving the invariant that the target, if present, is inside the window.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: It halves, not doubles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's not maintained; the window contains both larger and smaller values.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's quicksort's partition step.

easy.prompt: Counting sort can sort n integers in the range [0, k] in time…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Counting sort builds a frequency array of size k+1 in O(n+k) and writes the output in one pass.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the comparison-sort lower bound; counting sort beats it because it isn't comparison-based.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: There's no log factor in counting sort.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Counting sort is linear, not the product of n and k.

easy.prompt: What is the expected height of a randomly built BST on n distinct keys?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Inserting keys in random order produces a tree of expected height O(log n), even without explicit balancing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Square-root depth doesn't arise in BST analysis.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the worst-case height for adversarial insertion orders.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That would require a constant number of keys.

easy.prompt: Open addressing resolves a collision by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Re-hashing every key in the table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Storing colliding keys in a linked list at each slot.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Probing other slots in the table according to a fixed sequence.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Open addressing keeps every key in the table itself; on collision it probes alternate slots (linear, quadratic, double hashing).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Rehashing happens on resize, not on each collision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's separate chaining, not open addressing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Discarding would lose data; collisions must be resolved.

easy.prompt: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Merging the two least-frequent nodes into a new parent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Splitting the alphabet in half by frequency.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assigning shorter codes to the most-frequent symbols arbitrarily.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Huffman's greedy step always combines the two minimum-weight subtrees, producing an optimal prefix-free code.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Alphabetical order is irrelevant to code length.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a Shannon–Fano style top-down split, not Huffman.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Frequency rank alone doesn't yield an optimal code.

easy.prompt: What is the relationship between P and NP that's known (not conjectured)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: P is a subset of NP.

choices.label: C
choices.body: NP is a subset of P.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Every problem solvable in polynomial time is also verifiable in polynomial time, so P ⊆ NP. Whether the containment is strict is open.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Many problems (e.g., shortest path) are in both.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would mean P = NP, also unknown.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the famous open question; it isn't known to be true.

easy.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm uses which data structure to detect cycles efficiently?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Kruskal sorts edges by weight and adds each one only if its endpoints are in different components, tracked by union-find.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Prim's algorithm uses a priority queue; Kruskal doesn't.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Topological sort applies to DAGs, not undirected MSTs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Edges aren't hashed in Kruskal.

medium.prompt: If f(n) = 3n² + 10n + 50, which of the following is the tightest correct bound?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The dominant term is 3n², so f(n) is both O(n²) and Ω(n²) — hence Θ(n²).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: n² grows faster than n log n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: f grows slower than n³, so the lower bound is wrong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Linear is too small; the n² term dominates.

medium.prompt: Apply the Master Theorem: T(n) = 3 T(n/2) + n. What is T(n)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: a = 3, b = 2, so n^{log_b a} = n^{log₂ 3} ≈ n^{1.585}, which dominates f(n) = n. Case 1 applies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Linear would require f(n) to dominate, which it doesn't here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: n² grows faster than n^{1.585}; the recurrence doesn't reach it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's case 2, requiring f(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a}). Here log₂ 3 > 1.

medium.prompt: Why does the comparison-sort lower bound Ω(n log n) hold?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because mergesort runs in n log n time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because the input has n log n bits of entropy.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because every sort needs to copy the array at least log n times.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A decision tree distinguishing n! permutations has height at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Any deterministic comparison sort corresponds to a decision tree whose leaves are the n! permutations; height is at least the log of the leaf count.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's an upper-bound example, not a proof of the lower bound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Closer to right in spirit, but the formal argument is the decision-tree height.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: There's no such requirement; in-place sorts exist.

medium.prompt: In Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary-heap priority queue, the running time on a graph with V vertices and E edges is…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Each vertex is extracted once (O(log V)) and each edge triggers at most one decrease-key (O(log V)), giving (V+E) log V.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That omits the per-edge relaxation cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's Bellman–Ford's cost, not Dijkstra's with a heap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's Dijkstra with an array-based priority queue, which can be faster for dense graphs.

medium.prompt: What is the time and space complexity of the standard DP for the 0/1 knapsack with n items and capacity W?

choices.label: C
choices.body: O(2^n) time, since the problem is NP-hard.

choices.label: D
choices.body: O(nW) time and O(nW) space (reducible to O(W) space).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The pseudo-polynomial DP fills an n × W table; you can keep only the previous row to use O(W) space.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Too fast; each cell costs Θ(1) and there are nW of them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Far too fast; you must consider each item against each capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Knapsack is NP-hard in the input length, but DP runs in pseudo-polynomial time O(nW).

medium.prompt: Activity selection (max non-overlapping intervals) is optimally solved by greedily choosing…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The interval overlapping the fewest others.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The interval with the earliest start time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The interval with the earliest finish time among compatible ones.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Sorting by finish time and picking the earliest-finishing compatible interval leaves maximum room for the rest — exchange argument gives optimality.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sounds reasonable but doesn't optimize; finish-time greedy is the proven rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Earliest start can lock in a long interval that blocks many.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Counterexample exists: a short interval can block two longer compatible ones.

medium.prompt: Universal hashing guarantees what about collisions between two distinct keys x ≠ y?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pr[h(x) = h(y)] ≤ 1/m, taken over the random choice of h from the family.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every slot is hit exactly the same number of times.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Collisions only happen when keys are similar.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No two distinct keys ever collide.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: A family H is universal if, picking h uniformly at random from H, any pair of distinct keys collides with probability at most 1/m.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would require a specific input, not a family property.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Universality is independent of key similarity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's perfect hashing for a fixed set, not universal hashing in general.

medium.prompt: Bellman–Ford handles negative edge weights but rejects graphs with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: If a negative cycle is reachable, no shortest path is well-defined; Bellman–Ford detects this on the (V−1)+1-th relaxation pass.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unreachable vertices simply keep distance ∞.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Positive self-loops never affect shortest paths.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sinks are fine; the algorithm just doesn't relax through them.

medium.prompt: A min-heap supports which two operations in O(log n)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: find-min is O(1); insert and extract-min restore the heap property in O(log n) by sifting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: find-min is O(1), not O(log n).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: find-min is O(1); decrease-key is O(log n), but extract-min is the canonical second op.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: find-max requires scanning leaves — Θ(n) in a min-heap.

medium.prompt: What is the running time of the standard DP for the longest common subsequence of two strings of lengths m and n?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The DP fills an (m+1)×(n+1) table; each cell is O(1) work, giving Θ(mn) total.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Far too fast.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would require constant work per character of one string, but each cell depends on its row and column.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each cell is O(1), not O(mn).

medium.prompt: Strongly connected components of a directed graph can be found in linear time using…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Two DFS passes (Kosaraju's or Tarjan's algorithm).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Kosaraju runs DFS on G, then DFS on the transpose in reverse finishing order; both passes are O(V+E).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: BFS alone doesn't recover SCCs in directed graphs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Topological sort requires a DAG, which the graph may not be.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's O(V³) and unnecessary for SCCs.

medium.prompt: Quicksort's worst-case Θ(n²) running time occurs when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The pivot is chosen at random.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The recursion depth is log n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every partition is maximally unbalanced (e.g., already-sorted input with a deterministic pivot).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Picking the first or last element as pivot on sorted data forces partitions of size 1 and n−1, giving Θ(n²) work.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Random pivots give expected Θ(n log n) regardless of input.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random input gives expected Θ(n log n).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Log-depth recursion implies balanced partitions and Θ(n log n).

medium.prompt: The decision version of 3-SAT is NP-complete. What does that imply?

choices.label: B
choices.body: It is harder than every problem in NP.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It's in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It can be solved in polynomial time.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: NP-completeness means a problem is both in NP and NP-hard.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 3-SAT is decidable — brute force works in 2^n time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: It's at most as hard as the hardest NP problems, not strictly harder.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only if P = NP, which is open.

medium.prompt: For interval scheduling with weighted intervals, the earliest-finish-time greedy…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fails to give an optimal solution.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Once weights vary, greedy ignores the value tradeoff. The optimal algorithm is DP after sorting by finish time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No such bound; greedy can be arbitrarily bad here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Greedy is fast — the issue is correctness, not speed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights break the exchange argument that justified greedy in the unweighted case.

medium.prompt: What is the amortized cost per operation on a Fibonacci heap for extract-min, and for decrease-key?

choices.label: C
choices.body: O(log n) amortized for extract-min, O(1) amortized for decrease-key.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Fibonacci heaps' main benefit is O(1) amortized decrease-key, enabling Dijkstra in O(E + V log V).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Far too high for any heap of interest.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: extract-min still costs Θ(log n) amortized.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: decrease-key is O(1) amortized — that's the whole point of Fibonacci heaps.

medium.prompt: Radix sort using counting sort as a stable subroutine sorts n d-digit numbers in…

choices.label: B
choices.body: O(d (n + b)) where b is the radix.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Each of d passes runs counting sort in O(n + b); total is O(d(n+b)).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Radix avoids the comparison-sort lower bound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each pass is linear, not n log n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each pass is linear; total is linear in d.

medium.prompt: Floyd–Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths in time…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Three nested loops over V vertices give Θ(V³).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's V runs of Bellman–Ford.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Only enough for one source.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's one Dijkstra run with a heap; you'd need V of them for all-pairs.

medium.prompt: Top-down DP with memoization differs from bottom-up DP in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: It only works for problems with optimal substructure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It only computes subproblems actually reached by the recursion.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It runs in less asymptotic time.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Memoized recursion can skip unreachable cells of the DP table; bottom-up fills the whole table.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Optimal substructure is required for both styles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Asymptotically they match; constants differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both styles store subproblem solutions.

medium.prompt: Linear probing degrades sharply when…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Long runs of occupied slots form clusters; expected probe length grows like 1/(1−α)² as α → 1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Primes help linear probing, if anything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Key type is irrelevant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Universality helps, not hurts.

medium.prompt: A polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B shows…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A and B are equally hard.

choices.label: C
choices.body: B is at least as hard as A (up to polynomial factors).

choices.label: D
choices.body: A is at least as hard as B.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: If A reduces to B in poly time and B has a poly-time algorithm, so does A — so B is at least as hard.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Only if reductions exist in both directions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reduction doesn't say where B sits; only how A relates to it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The arrow goes the other way: reductions transfer hardness *to* the target.

hard.prompt: Suppose 3-SAT can be solved in time O(n^k) for some constant k. What follows?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: 3-SAT is NP-complete, so a polynomial-time algorithm for it implies polynomial-time algorithms for every NP problem via reduction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: P = NP implies NP = coNP, but the immediate consequence is P = NP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 3-SAT is not known to be in P; that's the open question.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only problems in NP would collapse; problems outside NP (e.g., undecidable ones) wouldn't.

hard.prompt: Bellman–Ford runs in O(VE) time. Why doesn't repeating the relaxation pass beyond V−1 iterations help?

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because the edge list is sorted by weight.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because each pass halves the remaining work.

choices.label: D
choices.body: After V−1 passes, all shortest paths (which have at most V−1 edges) are computed; further changes signal a negative cycle.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Any simple path has at most V−1 edges; V−1 relaxation rounds suffice unless a negative cycle keeps lowering some distance.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: It doesn't; it's an iterative relaxation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bellman–Ford doesn't require sorted edges.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each pass is O(E); work doesn't shrink.

hard.prompt: A graph is 2-colorable if and only if it…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: A graph is bipartite (i.e., 2-colorable) iff every cycle has even length; BFS layering proves it constructively.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Necessary but far from sufficient.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hamiltonicity is unrelated to chromatic number.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Many disconnected graphs are 2-colorable; many connected ones aren't.

hard.prompt: Quickselect (Hoare's) finds the k-th smallest in expected linear time. Why isn't the worst case linear?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Quickselect uses recursion, which is always slower than iteration.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Random pivots make the worst case exponential.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Adversarial inputs force unbalanced partitions giving Θ(n²); deterministic worst-case linear requires median-of-medians.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Plain Quickselect can degenerate to Θ(n²); median-of-medians chooses a guaranteed-balanced pivot for deterministic O(n).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Recursion isn't the issue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random pivots give expected linear, not exponential worst case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Median-of-medians achieves it.

hard.prompt: The edit-distance DP can be optimized from O(mn) space to O(min(m, n)) by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Recomputing on the fly without memoization.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Keeping only the previous row (or column) of the table.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Using a hash table instead of an array.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Each cell depends only on the cell above, left, and upper-left, so a single previous row suffices.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That blows running time up exponentially.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Greedy doesn't solve edit distance optimally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The same number of cells must still be computed.

hard.prompt: Cuckoo hashing guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup. What is the cost paid for this?

choices.label: C
choices.body: Insertions may trigger a rehash and are O(1) only amortized in expectation.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It only works on integer keys.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Cuckoo hashing's lookup probes a constant number of slots, but insertions can chain evictions and may need a full rehash.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Lookups always touch O(1) slots — that's the whole point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deletion is O(1) — just clear the slot you find the key in.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Any hashable key works.

hard.prompt: Max-flow equals min-cut in any flow network with a single source and sink — the…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: The max-flow min-cut theorem (Ford–Fulkerson, 1956) equates the value of a maximum flow with the capacity of a minimum s–t cut.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hall characterizes when a perfect matching exists in a bipartite graph.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: König relates max matching and min vertex cover in bipartite graphs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Menger relates max disjoint paths and min vertex/edge separators — a related but distinct result.

hard.prompt: Matroid theory characterizes problems where greedy is provably optimal: greedy works on (E, I) when…

choices.label: B
choices.body: (E, I) is a matroid — closed under subsets and satisfying the exchange property.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Edmonds showed that greedy maximization over (E, I) is correct iff (E, I) is a matroid.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Matroids are closed under taking subsets of independent sets, not intersections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Necessary for the problem to make sense, not sufficient.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Greedy on matroids works for any weights; negatives just get rejected.

hard.prompt: The class coNP consists of problems whose…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Algorithms run in randomized polynomial time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Solutions can be enumerated in polynomial space.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: NP verifies yes-instances; coNP verifies no-instances. Example: tautology is in coNP because a falsifying assignment certifies non-tautology.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's BPP or RP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's NP, not coNP.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's PSPACE.

hard.prompt: Union-find with union-by-rank and path compression supports m operations on n elements in time…

choices.label: D
choices.body: O(m α(n)) where α is the inverse Ackermann function.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Tarjan proved the amortized cost is Θ(α(n)) per operation, which is effectively constant for any conceivable n.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Strict O(1) per operation isn't achievable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Way too pessimistic for these heuristics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's union-by-rank alone, without path compression.

hard.prompt: An adversary lower-bound argument shows that finding the maximum of n elements needs at least…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Every non-maximum element must lose at least one comparison; with n−1 non-maxima, you need n−1 comparisons.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Not enough to eliminate n−1 non-maxima.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Far too few; each comparison eliminates only one candidate from being the max.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's a sort lower bound, not a max-finding bound.

hard.prompt: Why does selecting the median in linear time (median-of-medians) recurse on at most 7n/10 elements?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Roughly 3n/10 elements are guaranteed smaller and 3n/10 guaranteed larger than the chosen pivot.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because cache effects limit the recursion.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because the input is split exactly in half.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Grouping into fives and recursing on the median of medians leaves at most 7n/10 in either side of the partition.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Cache isn't part of the analysis.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: It isn't exactly half; the bound is 7n/10.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Median-of-medians is deterministic.

hard.prompt: Matrix-chain multiplication's DP runs in Θ(n³). Knuth's optimization brings it down to…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Θ(n²) using the monotonicity of split points.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Knuth–Yao speedup exploits the fact that the optimal split point is monotone, eliminating an n factor.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's exhaustive parenthesization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Far too fast; you must consider O(n²) subproblems.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No such bound is known here.

hard.prompt: Why is BFS not directly usable for shortest paths in graphs with non-negative weighted edges?

choices.label: A
choices.body: BFS only works on directed graphs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: BFS doesn't terminate on cyclic graphs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: BFS treats every edge as unit cost, so it minimizes hops rather than total weight.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: BFS layers reflect edge counts; weighted shortest paths need a priority queue (Dijkstra) or relaxation (Bellman–Ford).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: BFS works on both directed and undirected graphs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: BFS with a visited set always terminates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Plain BFS uses a FIFO queue.

hard.prompt: A Bloom filter trades exact membership for space efficiency. What kind of error can it make?

choices.label: A
choices.body: False negatives, but never false positives.

choices.label: B
choices.body: False positives, but never false negatives.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: An item known to be inserted always tests positive; items never inserted may collide on all hashed bits and falsely test positive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Reversed: if a bit was set on insert, it stays set.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inserts don't clear bits, so negatives are reliable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A Bloom filter isn't exact; that's the point.

hard.prompt: The PSPACE class contains problems solvable in polynomial space. The known containment chain is:
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Polynomial time is in polynomial space; NP and coNP are also in PSPACE (Savitch); PSPACE is in EXPTIME.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed inclusions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: All equalities are open; the first two are believed false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: EXPTIME is the largest of these; it isn't contained in NP.

hard.prompt: Strassen's algorithm multiplies two n×n matrices in time…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Seven recursive multiplications of n/2-sized blocks give T(n) = 7 T(n/2) + Θ(n²), solving to n^{log₂ 7}.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's the naive algorithm; Strassen beats it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Far below known lower bounds for matrix multiplication.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The Ω(n²) lower bound is open; no algorithm is known at n².

hard.prompt: Set Cover's greedy algorithm (pick the set covering most uncovered elements) achieves what approximation ratio?

choices.label: B
choices.body: An additive factor, independent of n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hₙ ≈ ln n (best possible unless P = NP).

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Greedy set cover is an (ln n)-approximation, and Feige showed no polynomial-time algorithm does asymptotically better unless P = NP.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Vertex cover is 2-approximable, not set cover in general.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: There's no additive bound known.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Set cover is NP-hard; no efficient exact algorithm is known.

hard.prompt: Skip lists achieve expected O(log n) search using…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Randomized layering — each node is promoted to higher levels with probability p.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Coin flips decide each node's tower height; the expected longest tower is Θ(log n), and search descends levels then walks forward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Skip lists don't hash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's dynamic arrays, not skip lists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's red-black or AVL trees.

hard.prompt: Edmonds–Karp implements Ford–Fulkerson with BFS to choose augmenting paths, giving running time…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: BFS finds shortest augmenting paths; at most O(VE) augmentations occur, each costing O(E).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a single BFS; max-flow needs many.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's MST or Dijkstra territory, not max-flow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ford–Fulkerson with poor pivots can be slow, but Edmonds–Karp is polynomial.
